name: Multiplication Table
description: Bizon the Champion isn't just charming, he also is very smart. While some of us were learning the multiplication table, Bizon the Champion had fun in his own manner. Bizon the Champion painted an n × m multiplication table, where the element on the intersection of the i -th row and j -th column equals i · j (the rows and columns of the table are numbered starting from 1). Then he was asked: what number in the table is the k -th largest number? Bizon the Champion always answered correctly and immediately. Can you repeat his success? Consider the given multiplication table. If you write out all n · m numbers from the table in the non-decreasing order, then the k -th number you write out is called the k -th largest number.
input_specification: The single line contains integers n , m and k (1 ≤ n , m ≤ 5·10 5 ; 1 ≤ k ≤ n · m ) .
output_specification: Print the k -th largest number in a n × m multiplication table.
approach_summary: Verify predicate monotonicity: P(x) is true for x ≤ K and false otherwise. Binary search over the answer domain to find the boundary in O(log(Range) × Verify_Time).

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 448D — Multiplication Table [33. Binary Search]
topic_editorial.summary: Binary search on the monotonic answer domain.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The predicate function $P(x)$ ('Is answer $\le x$ feasible?') is monotonic: if $P(x)$ is true for some value, it remains true for all larger values (or vice versa). This allows binary division of the answer search space $[\text{low}, \text{high}]$ in $O(\log(\text{Range}))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N \log(\text{Range}))$
  The binary search divides the search interval by 2 at each iteration, requiring $\log_2(\text{Range})$ steps. In each step, the feasibility check `check(mid)` scans the array in $\mathcal{O}(N)$ time.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(1)$ auxiliary space
  The algorithm operates directly over the input array without allocating extra auxiliary memory.
